title: Kratos phishing-as-a-service kit loses its battle with international law enforcement
teaser: Authorities neutralized a major phishing kit, leading to an arrest and billions of dollars in lost criminal revenue.
summary: International law enforcement, led by German agencies (ZIT and BKA) and supported by the US and Indonesia, successfully dismantled the highly dangerous Kratos phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) kit. This criminal tool allowed low-skill cybercriminals to bypass Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) by sending convincing, fake Microsoft-themed phishing pages to victims. The operation resulted in the arrest of the alleged developer in Indonesia and the neutralization of over 200 servers. Authorities estimate the scheme had targeted hundreds of thousands of victims across more than 30 countries and generated over €300,000 ($342,000) since 2024, having been used by over 1,800 criminal enterprises. German officials hailed the takedown as a major win for cybersecurity, sending a clear signal that phishing will not go unpunished.
content: Security Kratos phishing-as-a-service kit loses its battle with international law enforcement Alleged developer arrested in Indonesia after more than 200 servers slain German authorities say they have neutralized the main infrastructure supporting the Kratos phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) kit following an operation supported by the US and Indonesia. Officers from Frankfurt am Main's Central Office for Combating Internet Crime (ZIT) and the Federal Criminal Police (BKA) described Kratos as one of the most widespread and dangerous PhaaS kits on the market. In Indonesia, authorities said they arrested the Kratos kit's alleged "developer and technical administrator." The announcement of Kratos's takedown did not mention whether any other individuals are being pursued. According to the ZIT and BKA, Kratos allowed low-skill cybercrims to harvest credentials, including passwords and session cookies, to bypass MFA by providing them with convincing Microsoft-themed phishing pages. Criminals using Kratos phishing pages targeted hundreds of thousands of victims across more than 30 countries, while the operation behind the kit allegedly earned more than €300,000 ($342,000) since 2024. More than 1,800 criminal enterprises are estimated to have used Kratos, which was responsible for around 15,000 phishing campaigns per month. "Each individual campaign had the potential to harm several thousand recipients worldwide," the German authorities said in a statement. The operation neutralized more than 200 servers, according to the ZIT and BKA, although the latter declined to explain how. Methods used in previous takedowns included handing legal warrants to infrastructure providers, such as Kratos's chosen hosting company, and working with ISPs to null-route or sinkhole traffic associated with suspect IP addresses. Dr Benjamin Krause, head of the ZIT at the Frankfurt am Main Public Prosecutor's Office, said, "Our approach of disruptive law enforcement works: In addition to the primary task of identifying and prosecuting the accused, we have once again succeeded in dismantling a criminal online service and thus contributing to greater cybersecurity." Carsten Meywirth, head of the cybercrime department at the BKA, added: "Anyone who steals login credentials online using fake websites shouldn't feel safe. The success against the Kratos phishing kit shows that even highly professional phishing infrastructures can be effectively combated. "This is pioneering work and a clear signal to other cyber actors - phishing will not go unpunished and will be consistently fought by the BKA." Many names, same focus German authorities referred to the PhaaS kit only as Kratos, although open source reporting has tied it to products previously sold under names such as SneakyLog and Sneaky 2FA. Similarly, the ZIT and BKA mentioned only fake Microsoft authentication pages among the templates offered by Kratos. Microsoft, meanwhile, reported earlier this year that SneakyLog had been used to generate phishing campaigns targeting US citizens with fake W-2 tax forms . As recently as July 16, security shops such as Heal Security reported that Kratos offered customers lures themed around various websites, including SharePoint, OneDrive, Microsoft Forms, Canva, Tilda, and more. KnowBe4 added Adobe lures to that list with its own investigation in February, which also raised uncertainty about when the kit first hit the market. Microsoft, which said Kratos was also known as SneakyLog, believes the latter entered the phishing kit market as of early 2025, although KnowBe4 said the first signs of Kratos only emerged in January 2026. Muddying the picture further, KnowBe4 did not mention SneakyLog or Sneaky 2FA as part of Kratos's past. The security shop said instead that it evolved from a previous life as a family of commercial trojans and infostealers. One thing that most open source reports agree on, however, is that the targets of the phishing kit's customers are based primarily in the US and Europe. Microsoft identified manufacturing, retail, and healthcare as the main target industries in the US, while in Europe, industrial organizations, law firms, polytechnic institutions, schools, SMBs, and others have all been attacked, according to ANY.RUN . ®

title: Twitch will let parents stop their teens going live
teaser: Twitch parents now gain powerful controls to block streaming, manage time limits, and restrict content for their teens.
summary: Twitch has launched enhanced parental controls, giving guardians greater oversight of their 13- to 17-year-old children's activity on the streaming platform. Parents can link accounts to manage usage, receive weekly activity summaries, and block key features like live streaming or private messaging (Whispers). Furthermore, parents can enforce flexible daily time limits and restrict content based on classification labels, such as 'Gambling' or 'Mature-Rated Game.' These tools are accessible via the Account Settings under the Family Center. The system is designed to automatically unlink the user once they reach age 18, ensuring independence while maintaining parental safety features.
author: Jess Weatherbed
content: Twitch is giving parents more control over how their children are using the streaming platform, including the ability to block them from broadcasting entirely. Parental controls are now available that allow guardians to link Twitch accounts with their 13- to 17-year-old children, providing account management features and a weekly email summarizing their teen's activity, including channels and hours watched. The controls can be used to prevent teens from livestreaming their own content and disabling Whispers, Twitch's private messaging feature. This includes blocking minors from sending or receiving DMs. Parents can also set flexible daily time limits for Twitch across all their teen's devices and restrict content that carries certain classification labels - such as Gambling, Mature-Rated Game, Sexual Themes, and more - from appearing in searches or recommended feeds. The parental controls dashboard can be found in the Account Settings under the Family Center page. When a Twitch user managed by parental controls turns 18, their account will be automatically unlinked from their parents. Twitch says that it will explore adding additional parental control features in the future, noting that the setting is optional "at this time."

title: How investors learned to live with inflation
teaser: Investors are growing skeptical that central bankers can reliably bring inflation back to its target, signaling a major shift in economic expectations.
summary: Inflation management has become a key point of doubt, with fewer investors than ever believing that central banks can successfully restore inflation to its target level. This decline in confidence suggests a potential shift in economic doctrine, forcing both markets and investors to adapt their strategies to cope with sustained inflationary pressures. Instead of relying on historical central bank efficacy, the market is beginning to price in a new, more persistently inflationary normal.
content: Fewer than ever believe central bankers will bring it back to target

title: Apple teams up with Klarna to launch a lease-to-own program for iPhones, iPads, and Macs
teaser: Apple teams up with Klarna to launch 'Apple Upgrade,' making premium devices more accessible through multi-year lease-to-own plans.
summary:
To combat rising hardware prices and supply chain issues, Apple is launching 'Apple Upgrade,' a new lease-to-own program in partnership with Klarna. This service, launching around July 28th, allows consumers to pay for flagship devices like iPhones, iPads, Macs, and Apple Watches over multi-year terms (24-36 months). Unlike previous programs, this comprehensive initiative replaces old financing methods and aims to make premium devices more accessible. The program will allow users to keep or return devices at the end of the lease, with options for upgrades. 

*Jargon Explained:* A lease-to-own program functions like a car loan, allowing the user to use the device for a fixed period while paying installments, rather than making a large upfront purchase.

This strategic move comes shortly after Apple began raising prices on nearly all its product lines.
author: Lucas Ropek
content: Apple is reportedly teaming up with deferred payment processor Klarna to launch a new lease-to-own program for its devices. Bloomberg reported Tuesday that the program - dubbed Apple Upgrade - is set to launch next Tuesday. It will allow consumers to pay for their purchases over multi-year periods, including iPhones, iPads, Macs, and Apple Watches. Bloomberg writes that the lease term for iPhones and Apple Watches will be up to 24 months, while leases for Macs and iPads will be up to 36 months. The devices can either be kept or returned at the end of the leasing period, while upgrades to new devices will also be available (hence the name of the program). The report notes vaguely that, in some cases, "transactions will incur an additional fee." Apple already has a similar program called iPhone Upgrade, although the company plans to stop allowing new customer sign-ups to instead build out the broader, more inclusive Apple Upgrade program, the report said. A leasing program is an obvious move for Apple, at this point. The iPhone maker has been battling supply chain issues wrought by "RAMageddon" - the industry-wide shortage of memory chips that is driving up the price of hardware. Those shortages have been driven largely by the AI industry, which is gobbling up so much memory that it's not leaving much for the rest of us. To deal with these issues, Apple recently announced that it would be raising prices , and Upgrade clearly seems designed to make those hiked prices more palatable to consumers. TechCrunch reached out to Apple and Klarna for more information. Overall, the new program seems like a conservative move for Apple, which is currently facing a hectic transitional period. As new CEO John Ternus takes the reins, the company also made the decision to enter into a legal battle with AI startup superstar OpenAI - suing the company for alleged trade theft. In short: the company has its hands full, and anything that can shore up sales and keep the business headed in the right direction is a smart move.

title: The end of big teams🧑‍🤝‍🧑, China’s AI challenge🧠, and your AI diary 📓
teaser: AI is shifting the definition of ambition in Silicon Valley: big teams are out, efficient, smaller setups are in.
summary: AI is redefining corporate ambition in Silicon Valley, suggesting a pivot from building massive teams toward smaller, highly efficient workforces. This structural shift affects how 'hiring' and 'layoffs' are perceived in the market. Furthermore, the article advises development teams to challenge traditional requirements. Instead of assuming solutions, teams must focus on asking 'why'—identifying core needs—and testing small increments. This methodology helps teams retain flexibility and discover simpler, more effective answers.
author: TLDR Product
content: Is "jobs" a four-letter word? (5 minute read) AI is changing Silicon Valley's definition of ambition from building large teams to needing fewer people. This shift could make hiring look inefficient and layoffs look impressive. The Power Of "Why?" (3 minute read) Requirements often prescribe solutions instead of identifying real needs. Asking "why" and testing small increments helps teams preserve options and find simpler answers.

title: X Rebuilds Android 📱, Apple Tops Nvidia🍎, Agentio Comes to Meta 🤖
teaser: X relaunched its Android app after a year-long, massive engineering rebuild to improve reliability and enable future features.
summary: X, owned by Elon Musk, has relaunched its Android app following a year of significant effort. The new version was built entirely from scratch, rather than being a simple update, aiming for better loading, scrolling, notifications, and overall reliability. This effort is described as one of the largest engineering projects for the company, designed partly to strengthen X's presence in Android-heavy global markets. While improving the user experience, the app still has features under development, including better support for older Android devices, Spaces, a video editor, and cashtags. Users can now update via the Google Play Store.
author: TLDR Design
content: X relaunches a rebuilt Android app after year-long effort (2 minute read) X has relaunched its Android app after nearly a year of rebuilding it from scratch to improve loading, scrolling, notifications, reliability, and future feature development. The effort was described as one of the largest engineering projects in the company's history and is aimed partly at strengthening X in Android-heavy global markets. Some features are still unfinished, including better support for older devices, Spaces, video editing, react-with-video, cashtags, and custom timelines. Apple Briefly Became the World's Most Valuable Company, Toppling Nvidia (1 minute read) Apple briefly overtook Nvidia as the world's most valuable company after investors sold off AI-related semiconductor stocks, reflecting growing skepticism about the long-term returns of massive AI infrastructure spending. Unlike many of its rivals, Apple has spent relatively little on building AI infrastructure and instead benefits from its installed base of 2.5 billion devices. As a result, it is increasingly seen as well positioned to monetize AI features, especially after the positive reception to its revamped Siri. Agentio's AI-powered Creator Ads are Coming to Facebook and Instagram (2 minute read) Agentio, an AI-powered creator advertising platform previously focused on YouTube, has partnered with Meta to bring its tools to Facebook and Instagram. Brands can now access AI-driven insights, creator matching, and partnership ads across both platforms, with the option to run cross-platform campaigns spanning Meta and Google properties. Beta testing showed Agentio's Meta partnership ads achieved 81% higher ROAS and 89% higher click-through rates compared to brands' non-Agentio creator ads. Product Quality: A Shared Commitment to Craft in the Wake of AI (10 minute read) As AI collapses the gap between "nothing" and "adequate," genuine craft becomes the only remaining differentiator between products. Craft is a shared discipline across Utility, Usability, and Feel-owned collectively by engineers, PMs, designers, and leaders, not design alone. "Would I recommend this to someone I care about?" should be the standard for judging whether a product has truly earned people's affection, not just their approval. Why the Future of Design Must Begin with Understanding People (6 minute read) User experience has always extended beyond visible interfaces, shaped instead by trust, psychology, and human context. Drawing on architecture, emergency medical care, and design experience, the author contends AI heightens designers' responsibility to build informed-not blind-trust, making AI literacy an essential design skill. Design's future depends on understanding people rather than mastering tools, since technology changes but human needs remain constant. Accessibility Isn't a Checklist. It's a Design Decision You're Avoiding (14 minute read) A UX designer recounts watching a blind user struggle through an 11-minute flight booking process that should have taken 90 seconds, revealing how years of seemingly reasonable decisions had quietly excluded users with disabilities. The experience showed that accessibility isn't primarily a technical challenge or a compliance checklist-it requires making it a core product priority, testing with real assistive technology users, and treating accessibility as part of the definition of "done" rather than something to address later. AI Skills for Product Designers (Website) Whether you're directing your AI or working alongside it, Layers walks you through all seven layers of product design, so the decisions underneath the screen actually get made. Datatype (Website) Datatype is an OpenType variable font that turns simple text expressions into inline charts. No JavaScript, no images, and no rendering library. Against Design System Federation (6 minute read) Federated design system governance-used by just 13% of teams-is losing favor due to poor contribution rates, diffused accountability, and inflated cost-saving expectations. Layoffs and AI-driven productivity narratives have fueled interest in federation, but it typically damages system quality, user experience, and team morale rather than fixing organizational problems. Federation works best as one aspect within a hybrid model, not as a standalone governance approach, since it demands more organizational maturity than most companies achieve. The "mocked, then loved" AirPods effect (6 minute read) Apple's AirPods and Apple Watch both overcame early ridicule by proving genuinely useful in everyday life, but the rumored camera-equipped AirPods face a different challenge: concerns about privacy and social acceptance rather than just unconventional design. While Apple has a strong track record of turning skepticism into success, the new AirPods will need to demonstrate clear, hands-free AI benefits while convincing both wearers and those around them that the cameras can be trusted. Ask yourself where you can add value (2 minute read) Designers should stop undervaluing in-house work and instead showcase the business problems they solved, the constraints they worked within, and the measurable results they achieved. Rather than waiting to build a perfect portfolio, improve existing projects incrementally with stronger storytelling, updated visuals, and small enhancements, making steady progress in short bursts that fit around a busy schedule.

title: The Xteink X4 Pro could be the tiny e-reader of your dreams
teaser: The Xteink X4 Pro is a 5.95 mm thin e-reader with a touchscreen and front light, making pocketable reading more convenient than ever.
summary: Xteink has released the X4 Pro, a highly compact e-reader designed to fit in a wallet. This device, which weighs 72 grams and is 5.95 mm thin, significantly upgrades previous models by adding a much-needed touchscreen and adjustable front light, making it useful for nightly reading. Users can turn pages either by tapping the screen or using side buttons. Key features include excellent battery life—lasting weeks—and charging via a magnetic pogo charger. However, the device has limitations: it cannot directly integrate with library apps like Libby and is incompatible with Amazon's copyrighted e-books. The X4 Pro is priced at $99 and is available on Xteink's website.
author: Amanda Silberling
content: Xteink's tiny e-readers have gone viral among book lovers on social media, and for good reason: What could be more delightful than an e-reader that can fit in your wallet? Xteink has the answer. The Chinese hardware maker has now improved upon its existing e-readers with the Xteink X4 Pro , a swift response to widespread feedback from users who really wanted a touchscreen and a front light. If you haven't seen Xteink's existing X3 and slightly larger X4, let's catch you up to speed: They're likely the smallest e-readers you can buy; small enough to magnetize to the back of your phone or toss in your pocket on your way out the door. Ideally, having this device on hand will help you read a few pages of a book instead of scrolling Instagram while you're waiting in line at the store. Though the X3 and X4 were promising enough to cultivate a cult following, I wouldn't call them user friendly - their button-based navigation is clunky. Still, the idea of a magnetic, pocketable e-reader was so promising that I couldn't wait to see what Xteink would do next. Fortunately, the wait for a fix wasn't long. The addition of the touchscreen and front light makes the Xteink X4 Pro more viable as a device that you can use as your main e-reader, rather than just an on-the-go companion to your Kindle. At 72 grams and 5.95 mm thin, the X4 Pro is about the same size as the X4. Image Credits: Xteink Every night before I go to bed, I turn off the lights and read on my Kindle until I'm sleepy enough to close my eyes. But with the added front light, the X4 Pro has firmly wedged itself into my nightly routine - during the review period, I almost exclusively read on the X4 Pro before bed, using the front light on the dimmest setting (which is still a bit brighter than I'd like for bedtime reading), with the color temperature tinted slightly warm. I've since reverted back to my Kindle solely because I'm re-reading the Odyssey, and let's face it, it would be pretty annoying to read poetry with line breaks on a 4.26-inch screen. When I read with the X4 Pro before I fall asleep, I feel like I'm mimicking my old bad habit of scrolling in bed . You can interpret this as either a good or a bad thing. On one hand, this goes to show just how comfortable and easy it feels to read on the X4 Pro - you can turn the pages either by tapping on the side of the screen or by using the side buttons, which gives you more flexibility with how you want to hold your X4 Pro. But also, like a phone, the e-reader is so small that you have to hold it closer to your face to read than you would a Kindle. I worry this might impact my sleep, though it's still far easier to fall asleep after looking at a dimly lit e-ink screen than an iPhone. Like other e-ink devices, the X4 Pro has pretty great battery life - I've been using my device most days for about three weeks, and I'm only down to 60% battery. Naturally, the light means that the battery will dwindle a bit more quickly than its predecessors, but I barely notice the difference. What people will notice, however, is that the X4 Pro charges using a magnetic pogo charger, while the X4 had a USB-C. This isn't a big deal to me, since the device has to charge so infrequently, but if you're really passionate about the universality of USB-C, this could be a dealbreaker. Image Credits: Xteink The X4 Pro also comes with updated software, which is a big upgrade from the previous models, but the device also will continue to allow users to load open source code. The process of uploading content via Wi-Fi and Bluetooth is doable, though it remains a bit clunky - I find it easier to just remove the micro SD card and use the provided micro SD to USB adapter to add files from my computer. If you're used to more mainstream e-readers, it's also worth mentioning that you're probably not going to be able to read library e-books on the X4 Pro. Xteink can't integrate directly with apps like Libby, and even if you borrow an e-book from the library, you won't be able to add it to your X4 Pro (libraries use protected versions of .epub files that you can't copy). But if you buy an .epub file from a publisher, you'll be able to add it to your Xteink device without a problem. (Just don't try buying books on Amazon. It's a walled garden, so you can only read Amazon e-books on Amazon devices, even though you literally purchased the book! Booooo!) The Xteink X4 Pro costs $99, and at launch, it's only available on Xteink's website.

title: Windows 11 Start menu changes trickle into Beta, movable taskbar still MIA
teaser: Windows 11's redesigned Start menu is trickling into Beta, but the long-awaited movable taskbar—and lower system requirements—remain missing.
summary: Microsoft is rolling out more redesigned Start menu features to the Windows 11 Beta channel, including size controls and renaming 'Recommended' to 'Recent'. However, the highly requested ability to move the taskbar to different screen edges remains MIA, despite Microsoft's previous promises. Critics argue that instead of refining the UI, Microsoft should focus on significantly reducing Windows 11's system requirements. While Windows 10 can function with just 2 GB of RAM, Windows 11 requires a minimum of 4 GB. Addressing system resource needs for older PCs is seen as a more critical step than cosmetic Start menu tweaks.
content: os platforms Windows 11 Start menu changes trickle into Beta, movable taskbar still MIA Users asked for flexibility, but a leaner OS for older PCs might matter more as hardware prices soar Microsoft is moving more of its redesigned Start menu into the Windows 11 Beta channel, although the long-awaited movable taskbar remains confined to experimental builds. Build 26220.8925 was released last night to Windows Insiders in the Beta channel and has "a number of improvements for the Start menu," including controls for its size and sections. The Start menu has gained small and large size options alongside the existing default section-level toggles, a rename from Recommended to Recent, a redesigned Start menu settings page, and the option to hide the user's name and picture in Start. However, changing the location of the taskbar is not quite there yet despite pleas from users. In May, Microsoft stated : "Location, location, location. The ability to move the taskbar to the top or sides of the screen has been one of the most requested features, and we are bringing it to Windows 11." The ability to position the taskbar on any edge of the screen was familiar to Windows 10, but dropped from Windows 11 in the name of code rewrites. Users have complained ever since. Microsoft may hope that appearing to listen to taskbar feedback - rather than shoving more AI down customers' throats - might reverse some ill will toward its flagship operating system. It may be too little, too late. With hardware prices soaring, restoring interface features Microsoft should never have removed feels like small beer. A leaner Windows that runs well on older PCs would be far more useful. Windows 10 could work on 2 GB for 64-bit systems. Windows 11 needs at least 4 GB. Both represent a minimum, although some enterprising users have demonstrated just how low Windows 11 can go with all the cruft removed. Microsoft's Start menu fiddling has moved closer to production, hopefully with the taskbar changes following behind. However, if the Microsoft truly cares about user feedback, it will work on reducing Windows' system requirements while component costs remain painfully high. A movable taskbar might silence some complaints, but wider support for PCs that ran Windows 10 perfectly well would matter more to many users. ®

title: Peak Design’s modular Field Bracket has a finder tag built-in
teaser: Peak Design's Field Bracket solves the clutter problem, integrating a dual-platform tracking tag directly into a versatile L-bracket for photographers.
summary: Peak Design has launched its new Field Bracket system, a modular accessory designed for photographers and videographers. This innovative bracket combines the functionality of an L-bracket, hand grip, and cheese plate, allowing users to quickly adjust camera orientation and mount additional gear like lights or microphones. A major highlight is the integrated slot for the Beacon Finder Tag, which allows the tracking accessory to fit flush inside the base plate. This specific tag is compatible with both Apple Find My and Google Find Hub, ensuring universal coverage. Built to work with ARCA-compatible tripods, the system maintains camera strap attachment points and uses a 'Field Latch' for tool-free mounting. The bracket is priced at $149.95 MSRP, but is available at a discounted $125 during the Kickstarter campaign.
author: David Imel
content: I am a very clumsy man. So clumsy, that I have AirTags hanging off practically every camera I own. Have I left my camera in an Uber? Yes. Have I left it on an airplane? Also yes. For me, finder tags are essential for my cameras. The problem is, strapping a finder tag to a camera is always cumbersome. I currently have them hanging off my camera straps like a phone charm circa 2001. They're ugly, and very much get in the way when I'm trying to focus on shooting. But Peak Design thinks it has a solution in its new Field Bracket system, which it launched today on Kickstarter, starting at $150 for early birds . The Peak Design Field Bracket is part L-Bracket, part hand grip, part cheese plate. It's made for photographers and videographers who want to quickly switch between landscape and portrait orientation on their tripod, or sometimes want to mount a light or mic to their camera when there isn't a dedicated place to do so. But possibly the most enticing thing, to me at least, is that the bracket comes with a slot for a dedicated Finder Tag. Peak's Beacon Finder Tag is a Peak Design-branded finder that works with Apple Find My and Google Find Hub. That means it'll work with both Apple and Android phones, so you don't have to worry about losing access to your camera finder if you switch ecosystems. The tag uses a standard CR2025 battery, and Peak says it's rated to last up to 6 months. It's also rated for IP67 water and dust resistance, and it fits flush inside the base plate of the L-bracket. The Beacon Finder Tag is just one of the accessories Peak Design is selling alongside the Field Bracket. The base product you'll be buying is in fact an L-bracket, but once that's on your camera, you'll have access to other add-on accessories like a hand grip, finger grip, and cheese plate. Peak says the Field Bracket will work with most ARCA-compatible tripods, and won't get in the way if you use it with its own capture clip or camera straps. In fact, the bracket itself has dedicated slots to attach your Peak Design camera strap, so you won't have to sacrifice the strap you own to use the bracket. Peak calls the vertical attachment to the L-bracket the Field Latch, and it uses the company's new locking system to quickly attach and detach it without any tools. This is the same place you attach the optional cheese plate, which pulls out in adjustable stops in case you need to access ports or run cables from the camera. Of course, you'll have to choose the exact bracket you want for the camera you own, considering it's molded specifically to that body. At launch, most cameras supported are the newest, or near-newest models of each camera line. You can see a compatibility list here . And if you want to see your camera supported, Peak has a dedicated feedback page to submit the camera you own. The bracket itself will MSRP at $149.95, and if you want a bundle of all the accessories currently offered, you can get everything for $269.80. As usual, though, Peak Design is offering a Kickstarter discount, which puts the bracket at $125 and the bundle at $199, while supplies last at least.

title: Nearly every Kindle is steeply discounted at Best Buy
teaser: Looking for an e-reader? Best Buy's 'Black Friday in July' sale discounts nearly every Kindle, including the Paperwhite for an all-time low of $124.99.
summary: Best Buy is holding a 'Black Friday in July' sale, heavily discounting various Kindle e-readers. The waterproof Kindle Paperwhite, recommended for most users, is marked down to $124.99. Other deals include the Kindle Kids at $99.99, which adds kid-friendly extras. For color enthusiasts, the Kindle Colorsoft starts at $159.99, featuring a color E Ink display. The Kindle Scribe and Scribe Colorsoft are available starting at $379.99 and $479.99, respectively, offering 11-inch displays and included styluses for digital note-taking and annotating. The Scribe Colorsoft is best for color-coded notes or documents.
author: Sheena Vasani
content: If you've been thinking about picking up a Kindle before school starts, or for your next vacation, now's a good time to do it. As part of its Black Friday in July sale, Best Buy has brought the Kindle Paperwhite back down to its all-time low of $124.99 ($35 off) . It's the Kindle we recommend for most people because it has a bunch of features. It's waterproof and features a sharp 300ppi, 7-inch display, it offers an adjustable warm light for reading at night, and it has great battery life that can last for more than a month on a single charge. Best Buy has also discounted nearly every other Kindle model. The Kindle Kids is a good deal even for adults. It's down to $99.99 ($30 off) , and includes the same hardware as the standard Kindle, but with some extras: a kid-friendly cover, no ads, a two-year worry-free guarantee, and six months of Amazon Kids Plus. If you read comics, the Kindle Colorsoft is also on sale starting at $159.99 ($90 off) . It shares many of the Paperwhite's strengths but adds a color E Ink display that displays color at up to 150ppi. The Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition , which has 32GB of storage and wireless charging, is on sale for $219.99 ($60 off) . If you want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook, the Kindle Scribe and Kindle Scribe Colorsoft are worth considering. They're on sale starting at $379.99 ($120 off) and $479.99 ($150 off) , respectively. Each offers an 11-inch display with an included stylus for writing notes, annotating Kindle books, and marking documents. They also include notebook templates and AI-powered tools that can summarize notes or clean up messy handwriting. The biggest difference is that the Scribe Colorsoft adds a color E Ink display, making it a better choice for reviewing color documents or organizing notes with different colors.
